questions.q: A rigid container holds an unknown gas. A student measures the pressure of the gas and its temperature in kelvins. Which additional quantity must the student know to calculate the number of moles of gas in the container?
options: The molar mass of the gas
The diameter of a gas molecule
The volume of the container
The mass of the gas sample
optionWhy: A student who thinks the identity of a gas changes the gas law picks this. PV = nRT applies to every ideal gas with the same R; molar mass is needed only to convert moles to grams.
A student who thinks larger molecules mean fewer moles fit in a container picks this. Gas molecules take up a negligible part of the volume, so their size does not enter n = PV/RT.
Rearranging PV = nRT gives n = PV/RT. With P and T measured and R a constant, the volume of the container is the only missing quantity.
A student who reads n in PV = nRT as the mass of gas picks this. The mass would give moles only with the molar mass, which is unknown; with P and T known, the volume gives n directly.
questions.explain: Rearranging PV = nRT gives n = PV/RT. With P and T measured and R a constant, the volume of the container is the only missing quantity.
questions.working: n = PV/RT. P and T are measured and R is a constant, so the only additional quantity needed is V, the volume of the container (which, for a gas, is the volume of the gas). The molar mass, molecular size and sample mass do not appear in n = PV/RT.

questions.q: A fixed amount of an ideal gas is kept at constant pressure. Which of the numbered graphs best represents the volume of the gas as a function of its temperature in degrees Celsius?
options: Graph 1
Graph 2
Graph 3
Graph 4
optionWhy: A student who treats volume as proportional to Celsius temperature picks this line through 0°C. At 0°C (273 K) a gas still has a substantial volume; zero is reached only at −273°C.
A student who thinks volume is inversely related to temperature picks this falling curve. At constant pressure a gas expands as it is heated: V rises with T.
A student who thinks the volume of a gas depends only on its amount picks this flat line. With n and P fixed, V changes in proportion to Kelvin temperature.
At constant n and P, V is proportional to Kelvin temperature, so against Celsius temperature the graph is a straight line that would reach zero volume at −273°C (0 K) and is above zero at 0°C.
questions.explain: At constant n and P, V is proportional to Kelvin temperature, so against Celsius temperature the graph is a straight line that would reach zero volume at −273°C (0 K) and is above zero at 0°C.
questions.working: V = (nR/P)T with T in kelvins, so V is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature. In degrees Celsius, T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15, so V plotted against T(°C) is a straight line that reaches V = 0 at −273°C, not at 0°C.

questions.q: An aqueous solution of acetic acid is at equilibrium at constant temperature: CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). Which statement best describes the proton transfers occurring in the solution?
options: Protons have stopped passing between the species now that equilibrium is reached.
Protons pass from CH₃COOH to H₂O, and pass back only if the solution is cooled.
Protons pass from CH₃COOH to H₂O, and H₃O⁺ does not pass protons to CH₃COO⁻.
Protons pass from CH₃COOH to H₂O and from H₃O⁺ to CH₃COO⁻ at equal rates.
optionWhy: A student who thinks reactions stop at equilibrium picks this. The concentrations are constant because protons are transferred in both directions at equal rates, not because transfer has stopped.
A student who thinks a reversible process goes in reverse only when the conditions change picks this. The reverse transfer, from H₃O⁺ to CH₃COO⁻, takes place continuously at constant temperature.
A student who thinks proton transfer goes only from the acid to the base picks this. H₃O⁺ is itself an acid and CH₃COO⁻ can accept a proton, so the reverse transfer occurs too.

The forward reaction transfers protons from CH₃COOH to H₂O, and the reverse reaction transfers protons from H₃O⁺ back to CH₃COO⁻. At equilibrium both transfers continue at equal rates, so the concentrations stay constant.
questions.explain: The forward reaction transfers protons from CH₃COOH to H₂O, and the reverse reaction transfers protons from H₃O⁺ back to CH₃COO⁻. At equilibrium both transfers continue at equal rates, so the concentrations stay constant.

questions.q: A small amount of liquid water is placed in an evacuated flask, which is then sealed and kept at constant temperature. The pressure of water vapor in the flask rises and then becomes constant while some liquid remains. Which of the following best explains why the pressure stops rising?
options: Water molecules now return to the liquid at the same rate that they leave it.
Water molecules have stopped moving between the liquid and the vapor.
Water molecules have filled the space, leaving no room for more vapor.
Water molecules leave the liquid and return to it by turns, not at the same time.
optionWhy: Evaporation continues, while the rate of condensation increases as vapor builds up. Once molecules return to the liquid as often as they leave it, the number of molecules in the vapor, and so the pressure, stays constant.
A student who thinks nothing happens at equilibrium picks this. Molecules keep evaporating and condensing; the pressure is constant because the two processes occur at equal rates.
A student who thinks evaporation stops when the space above the liquid is full picks this. The space is mostly empty; the pressure stops rising because condensation has become as fast as evaporation.
A student who thinks the forward and reverse processes take turns picks this. Evaporation and condensation occur at the same time, in different molecules, at equal rates.
questions.explain: Evaporation continues, while the rate of condensation increases as vapor builds up. Once molecules return to the liquid as often as they leave it, the number of molecules in the vapor, and so the pressure, stays constant.

questions.q: The reversible reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) takes place in a sealed, rigid container at constant temperature. The particulate diagrams show the same small region of the container at four successive times. Which statement correctly describes the reactions in the container between time 3 and time 4?
options: The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction
The reverse reaction is now faster than the forward reaction
The forward and reverse reactions have both come to a stop
The forward and reverse reactions are occurring at equal rates
optionWhy: A student who reads 'more B than A' as 'the forward reaction is faster' picks this. If the forward reaction were faster, the number of B particles would still be rising; it stays at 8, so the rates are equal.

A student who thinks the substance present in the larger amount must react faster picks this, because there are twice as many B particles as A particles. If the reverse reaction were faster, the number of A particles would rise; it stays at 4, so the rates are equal.

A student who thinks reactions stop at equilibrium picks this, because the numbers of A and B no longer change. A and B are both still present, so both reactions continue; the numbers stay constant because the two reactions occur at equal rates.

From time 1 to time 3 the number of A particles falls (10, 7, 4) and the number of B particles rises (2, 5, 8): a net conversion of A to B, so the forward rate is the greater. Between time 3 and time 4 the numbers stay at 4 A and 8 B, so there is no net conversion: the forward and reverse reactions are occurring at equal rates.
questions.explain: From time 1 to time 3 the number of A particles falls (10, 7, 4) and the number of B particles rises (2, 5, 8): a net conversion of A to B, so the forward rate is the greater. Between time 3 and time 4 the numbers stay at 4 A and 8 B, so there is no net conversion: the forward and reverse reactions are occurring at equal rates.

questions.q: A sample of colorless N₂O₄(g) is placed in a sealed, rigid flask at constant temperature, where the reaction N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2 NO₂(g) occurs. NO₂(g) is brown. The brown color of the mixture deepens for several minutes and then stops changing. Which claim about the period during which the color is deepening is best supported?
options: NO₂ forms but is not yet consumed, so the reverse reaction has not yet begun
NO₂ forms faster and faster, so the forward rate rises until the color stops changing
NO₂ forms faster than it is used up, so the forward reaction is the faster one
NO₂ is used up at a rising rate, so the reverse rate exceeds the forward rate
optionWhy: A student who thinks the reverse reaction starts only once equilibrium is reached picks this. As soon as some NO₂ is present it begins to react to form N₂O₄; the color deepens because NO₂ forms faster than it is consumed.

A student who thinks the forward reaction speeds up as a reaction approaches equilibrium picks this. The forward rate falls as N₂O₄ is used up; the color stops changing when the falling forward rate and the rising reverse rate become equal.

A deepening brown color shows that the amount of NO₂ is increasing: there is a net conversion of N₂O₄ to NO₂. That happens when the forward reaction, which forms NO₂, is faster than the reverse reaction, which consumes it.

A student who takes a rising reverse rate to mean that the reverse reaction is the faster one picks this. The reverse rate does rise as NO₂ accumulates, but while the color is deepening it is still smaller than the forward rate.
questions.explain: A deepening brown color shows that the amount of NO₂ is increasing: there is a net conversion of N₂O₄ to NO₂. That happens when the forward reaction, which forms NO₂, is faster than the reverse reaction, which consumes it.

questions.q: A rigid 2.0 L container holds a mixture of the gases N₂, H₂ and NH₃, which react according to the equation N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g). The table shows the amount of each gas in the container at a particular moment. What is the value of Q_c at that moment?
optionWhy: A student who writes the quotient without exponents picks this: 0.30/((0.75)(0.50)) = 0.80. Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient, which gives (0.30)²/((0.75)(0.50)³) = 0.96.
The concentrations are [N₂] = 0.75 M, [H₂] = 0.50 M and [NH₃] = 0.30 M. Q_c = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³) = (0.30)²/((0.75)(0.50)³) = 0.96.
A student who multiplies each concentration by its coefficient picks this: (2 × 0.30)/((0.75)(3 × 0.50)) = 0.53. The coefficients are exponents, not multipliers, which gives 0.96.
A student who puts the amounts in moles into the expression picks this: (0.60)²/((1.5)(1.0)³) = 0.24. Q_c uses concentrations, so each amount must first be divided by 2.0 L, which gives 0.96.
questions.explain: The concentrations are [N₂] = 0.75 M, [H₂] = 0.50 M and [NH₃] = 0.30 M. Q_c = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³) = (0.30)²/((0.75)(0.50)³) = 0.96.

questions.q: A student mixes solutions of A and B, with no C present, to study the hypothetical reaction A(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ C(aq) at constant temperature. The student measures the concentrations at regular intervals and calculates Q_c each time. Which of the numbered graphs best represents how the calculated values of Q_c are expected to change with time?
options: Graph 1
Graph 2
Graph 3
Graph 4
optionWhy: A student who thinks the reaction quotient always has the value of the equilibrium constant picks this graph. Q_c depends on the concentrations at each moment: it is zero when no C is present and equals K_c only once equilibrium is reached.

A student who writes the quotient as reactants over products picks this graph, expecting a very large value when only A and B are present. With products in the numerator, Q_c starts at zero and increases toward K_c.

A student who thinks the reaction continues until the reactants are used up picks this graph, in which Q_c rises past K_c. The net reaction stops when Q_c reaches K_c, so Q_c levels off at that value.

With no C present at the start, Q_c = [C]/([A][B]) is zero. As C forms and A and B are used up, Q_c increases; the reaction quotient tends toward the equilibrium constant, and once Q_c = K_c the concentrations, and so Q_c, stay constant.
questions.explain: With no C present at the start, Q_c = [C]/([A][B]) is zero. As C forms and A and B are used up, Q_c increases; the reaction quotient tends toward the equilibrium constant, and once Q_c = K_c the concentrations, and so Q_c, stay constant.

questions.q: The hypothetical reaction X(g) + Y(g) ⇌ 2 Z(g) is allowed to reach equilibrium in a rigid container at a constant temperature. The table shows the concentrations measured in the equilibrium mixture. What is the value of K_c for the reaction at this temperature?
optionWhy: K_c = [Z]²/([X][Y]) = (0.15)²/((0.35)(0.70)) = 0.0225/0.245 = 0.092. The coefficient 2 of Z becomes the exponent on [Z].
A student who leaves the coefficients out of the equilibrium expression picks this: 0.15/((0.35)(0.70)) = 0.61. Because the coefficient of Z is 2, [Z] must be squared.
A student who uses the coefficient of Z as a multiplier picks this: (2 × 0.15)/((0.35)(0.70)) = 1.2. In an equilibrium expression a coefficient of 2 becomes an exponent: [Z]², not 2[Z].

A student who puts the reactant concentrations over the product concentration picks this: (0.35)(0.70)/(0.15)² = 11. K_c has the products of the reaction as written in the numerator, so the value is the reciprocal, 0.092.
questions.explain: K_c = [Z]²/([X][Y]) = (0.15)²/((0.35)(0.70)) = 0.0225/0.245 = 0.092. The coefficient 2 of Z becomes the exponent on [Z].
questions.working: K_c = [Z]²/([X][Y]) = (0.15)²/((0.35)(0.70)) = 0.0225/0.245 = 0.092. Distractors: exponent omitted, 0.15/0.245 = 0.61; coefficient used as a multiplier, (2 × 0.15)/0.245 = 1.2; expression inverted, 0.245/0.0225 = 11.

questions.q: A sample of the hypothetical gas A is placed in an evacuated rigid container at constant temperature, where it reacts according to the equation 2 A(g) ⇌ B(g). The graph shows [A] and [B] as functions of time. Based on the graph, what is the value of K_c for the reaction at this temperature?
optionWhy: A student who thinks equilibrium is reached where the reactant and product concentrations are equal picks this, using the crossing point: 0.25/(0.25)² = 4.0. At the crossing point both curves are still changing; equilibrium is where they level off, at [A] = 0.15 M and [B] = 0.30 M.
The curves level off after about 40 s, so the equilibrium concentrations are [A] = 0.15 M and [B] = 0.30 M. K_c = [B]/[A]² = 0.30/(0.15)² = 13.
A student who puts the starting concentration of A into the expression picks this: 0.30/(0.75)² = 0.53. K_c uses the [A] remaining at equilibrium, 0.15 M, because 0.60 M of A has reacted.
A student who puts the reactant term over the product term picks this: (0.15)²/0.30 = 0.075. For 2 A ⇌ B, K_c = [B]/[A]², the reciprocal of this value.
questions.explain: The curves level off after about 40 s, so the equilibrium concentrations are [A] = 0.15 M and [B] = 0.30 M. K_c = [B]/[A]² = 0.30/(0.15)² = 13.
questions.working: Both curves are level after about 40 s, so the equilibrium values are [A] = 0.15 M and [B] = 0.30 M (check: 0.75 − 0.15 = 0.60 M of A reacted, forming 0.30 M B, ratio 2:1). K_c = [B]/[A]² = 0.30/(0.15)² = 0.30/0.0225 = 13. Distractors: values at the crossing point (both 0.25 M), 0.25/(0.25)² = 4.0; starting [A] used, 0.30/(0.75)² = 0.53; expression inverted, (0.15)²/0.30 = 0.075.

questions.q: The table gives data for four hypothetical reactions at 25°C. Each reaction has the form R(aq) ⇌ P(aq), and each is started with R only. Which reaction proceeds essentially to completion?
options: Reaction 1
Reaction 2
Reaction 3
Reaction 4
optionWhy: A student who thinks K is the fraction of reactant converted, so that K_c = 1.0 means complete conversion, picks this. K_c = [P]/[R] = 1.0 means equal concentrations of P and R at equilibrium, so only about half of the R has reacted.

Each reaction has the form R ⇌ P, so K_c = [P]/[R] at equilibrium. Reaction 2 has K_c = 6 × 10¹², so at equilibrium [P] is about 10¹² times [R]: essentially all of the R has been converted to P. Its long time to reach equilibrium describes the rate, not the extent, of the reaction.

A student who thinks a reaction that reaches equilibrium quickly must go far toward products picks this, because Reaction 3 is the fastest. Its K_c of 0.20 means [P] is only one-fifth of [R] at equilibrium; how fast equilibrium is reached does not tell how far the reaction goes.

A student who reads a large negative exponent as a large number picks this, because 10⁻¹⁴ has the largest exponent in the table. 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ is a very small number, so in Reaction 4 [P] is only about 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ times [R]: the reaction barely proceeds.

questions.q: For the reaction N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2 NO(g), the value of K_c at 25°C is of the order of 10⁻³⁰. A sealed container of N₂(g) and O₂(g) is kept at 25°C until equilibrium is reached. Which claim about the contents of the container at equilibrium, and its justification, is correct?
options: N₂, O₂ and NO are present in equal amounts, because the system is at equilibrium
Almost all of the N₂ and O₂ has become NO, because the system is at equilibrium
No NO at all is present, because a reaction with so small a K_c does not occur
Only a very small amount of NO is present, because K_c is extremely small
optionWhy: A student who thinks reactants and products are present in equal amounts at equilibrium picks this. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal; with K_c about 10⁻³⁰ the amount of NO is tiny compared with the amounts of N₂ and O₂.

A student who thinks that reaching equilibrium means the reaction has gone to completion picks this. Being at equilibrium means only that there is no further net change; the very small K_c shows that the equilibrium lies far toward N₂ and O₂.

A student who thinks a reaction with a very small K does not occur at all picks this. A very small K means the reaction barely proceeds: NO is present at equilibrium, at a very low concentration, because both the forward and reverse reactions occur.

K_c = [NO]²/([N₂][O₂]) is about 10⁻³⁰, so at equilibrium [NO]² is about 10⁻³⁰ times [N₂][O₂]. The reaction barely proceeds: the mixture is almost entirely N₂ and O₂, with a very small but nonzero concentration of NO.
questions.explain: K_c = [NO]²/([N₂][O₂]) is about 10⁻³⁰, so at equilibrium [NO]² is about 10⁻³⁰ times [N₂][O₂]. The reaction barely proceeds: the mixture is almost entirely N₂ and O₂, with a very small but nonzero concentration of NO.
questions.working: No calculation needed. K_c = [NO]²/([N₂][O₂]) ≈ 10⁻³⁰, far less than 1, so at equilibrium [NO]² is about 10⁻³⁰ times [N₂][O₂]: the reaction barely proceeds and NO is present only at a very low concentration, but not zero.

questions.q: For the hypothetical reaction 2 X(g) + Y(g) ⇌ 2 Z(g), K_c = 0.020 at a certain temperature. What is the value of K_c for the reaction 2 Z(g) ⇌ 2 X(g) + Y(g) at the same temperature?
optionWhy: A student who thinks K is unchanged when a reaction is reversed picks this. Reversing the equation swaps the numerator and denominator of the expression, so K_c becomes 1/0.020 = 50.
A student who applies the ΔH rule for reversing a reaction to K picks this. K is a ratio of concentrations and cannot be negative; reversing the reaction inverts it, giving 50.
The second equation is the reverse of the first, so its equilibrium expression is the reciprocal of the original: K_c = 1/0.020 = 50.

A student who thinks K is the fraction of reactant converted, so that the reverse reaction converts the rest, picks this: 1 − 0.020 = 0.98. K is a ratio of equilibrium concentrations, and the reverse reaction has K_c = 1/0.020 = 50.
questions.explain: The second equation is the reverse of the first, so its equilibrium expression is the reciprocal of the original: K_c = 1/0.020 = 50.
questions.working: The second equation is the first reversed, so K_c = 1/0.020 = 50. Distractors: K unchanged, 0.020; sign changed as for ΔH, −0.020; 1 − K as if K were the fraction converted, 1 − 0.020 = 0.98.

questions.q: For the hypothetical reaction A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), K_c = 4.0 at a certain temperature. At one moment, a reaction mixture at this temperature has Q_c = 25. Which statement correctly describes the mixture at that moment?
options: The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction, so [C] rises
The forward and reverse reactions are equally fast, so [C] stays the same
Only the reverse reaction occurs, and it continues until Q_c equals K_c
The reverse reaction is faster than the forward reaction, so [C] decreases
optionWhy: A student who reverses the meaning of the Q–K comparison picks this. When Q > K, there is already too much product relative to reactants, so the net reaction consumes C, not forms it.
A student who thinks any mixture containing reactants and products is at equilibrium picks this. The rates are equal only when Q = K; here Q_c = 25 is not equal to K_c = 4.0.

A student who thinks only one reaction occurs while a system moves toward equilibrium picks this. Both reactions occur; the reverse reaction is faster, so the net change is toward A and B until the two rates become equal.

Q_c = 25 is greater than K_c = 4.0, so the ratio [C]/([A][B]) is too large. The reverse reaction is faster than the forward reaction, so there is a net consumption of C and formation of A and B until Q_c = K_c.
questions.explain: Q_c = 25 is greater than K_c = 4.0, so the ratio [C]/([A][B]) is too large. The reverse reaction is faster than the forward reaction, so there is a net consumption of C and formation of A and B until Q_c = K_c.
questions.working: No calculation needed beyond the comparison. Q_c = 25 > K_c = 4.0, so the mixture contains too much C relative to A and B: the reverse reaction is faster than the forward reaction, and the net change consumes C and forms A and B until Q_c falls to 4.0. Both reactions occur throughout.

questions.q: Pure A(g) is placed in a sealed, rigid container at constant temperature, where the reversible reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) takes place. The diagrams represent the contents of the container at four successive times, t₀ to t₃. Which statement about the system is supported by the diagrams?
options: It is at equilibrium at t₁ alone, as the numbers of A and B are equal at that time
It has been at equilibrium since t₁, as A and B are both present from then on
It has not reached equilibrium by t₃, as particles of A are still present at t₃
It reached equilibrium by t₂, as its composition is the same in the t₂ and t₃ diagrams
optionWhy: A student who thinks equilibrium means equal numbers of reactant and product particles picks this. The composition is still changing after t₁ (5 A and 5 B become 3 A and 7 B), so t₁ is not equilibrium; equilibrium is the unchanging mixture at t₂ and t₃.

A student who thinks any mixture containing both reactant and product is at equilibrium picks this. Between t₁ and t₂ the numbers still change, so the system reaches equilibrium only when the composition becomes constant, at 3 A and 7 B.

A student who thinks a reaction reaches equilibrium only when the reactant is used up picks this. In a reversible reaction reactant remains at equilibrium; the unchanged counts at t₂ and t₃ show that equilibrium has been reached.

The diagrams show 10 A at t₀, 5 A and 5 B at t₁, and 3 A and 7 B at both t₂ and t₃. A composition that no longer changes, with reactant and product both present, is what a particulate diagram of an equilibrium mixture shows.
questions.explain: The diagrams show 10 A at t₀, 5 A and 5 B at t₁, and 3 A and 7 B at both t₂ and t₃. A composition that no longer changes, with reactant and product both present, is what a particulate diagram of an equilibrium mixture shows.

questions.q: The hypothetical reaction D(g) + E(g) ⇌ G(g) is at equilibrium in a rigid container with [D] = 0.20 M. More D(g) is then injected, which raises [D] to 0.50 M at the moment of injection. Which statement describes [D] once equilibrium is re-established at the same temperature?
options: It stays at 0.50 M, its value just after the injection
It settles at a value between 0.20 M and 0.50 M
It rises to some value that is greater than 0.50 M
It returns to 0.20 M, its value before the injection
optionWhy: A student who thinks an added substance simply stays in the mixture, with no net reaction, picks this. The injection makes Q less than K, so a net forward reaction consumes some of the D.

The added D makes Q less than K, so a net forward reaction uses up some D and [D] falls below 0.50 M. The stress is only partly counteracted: if [D] fell all the way to 0.20 M, with less E and more G than before, Q would exceed K.
A student who thinks an equilibrium shifts toward the side to which a substance is added picks this, expecting still more D to form. Adding D causes the net forward reaction, which consumes D.

A student who thinks the system completely undoes a stress picks this. The net reaction removes only part of the added D; a return to 0.20 M with less E and more G than before would make Q greater than K.
questions.explain: The added D makes Q less than K, so a net forward reaction uses up some D and [D] falls below 0.50 M. The stress is only partly counteracted: if [D] fell all the way to 0.20 M, with less E and more G than before, Q would exceed K.
questions.working: Just after the injection Q < K, so a net forward reaction consumes D and E and forms G: [D] falls below 0.50 M. It cannot fall as far as 0.20 M: with [D] back at 0.20 M, [E] lower and [G] higher than originally, Q = [G]/([D][E]) would be greater than K. So 0.20 M < [D] < 0.50 M.

questions.q: The hypothetical reaction 2 X(g) ⇌ Y(g) reached equilibrium in a rigid container at constant temperature. Additional Y(g) was then injected into the container. The table shows the concentrations of X and Y at equilibrium and immediately after the injection. What is the value of the reaction quotient, Q, immediately after the injection?
optionWhy: A student who thinks Q equals K at every moment picks this, the value of K = 0.500/(0.250)². The injection changed [Y], so Q immediately afterward is 1.25/(0.250)² = 20.0, not K.

Q has the same form as K, Q = [Y]/[X]², but uses the concentrations present at the moment in question. Immediately after the injection, Q = 1.25/(0.250)² = 20.0, which is greater than K = 0.500/(0.250)² = 8.00, so the system is no longer at equilibrium.
A student who writes Q without powers picks this: 1.25/0.250 = 5.00. The coefficient 2 for X makes the denominator [X]², so Q = 1.25/(0.250)² = 20.0.
A student who uses the coefficient as a multiplier picks this: 1.25/(2 × 0.250) = 2.50. In Q the coefficient is an exponent, so the denominator is (0.250)² and Q = 20.0.
questions.explain: Q has the same form as K, Q = [Y]/[X]², but uses the concentrations present at the moment in question. Immediately after the injection, Q = 1.25/(0.250)² = 20.0, which is greater than K = 0.500/(0.250)² = 8.00, so the system is no longer at equilibrium.
questions.working: Q = [Y]/[X]² for 2 X ⇌ Y. Immediately after the injection, Q = 1.25/(0.250)² = 1.25/0.0625 = 20.0. (For comparison, K = 0.500/(0.250)² = 8.00, so Q > K and the net reaction will proceed toward X.)

options: Diagram 1
Diagram 2
Diagram 3
Diagram 4
optionWhy: A student who thinks the subscript 2 means F₂ units stay together picks the box with joined pairs of F⁻. Each formula unit that dissolves gives two separate F⁻ ions; there are no F₂ particles in the solution.

questions.q: The hypothetical salt MX₂ dissolves according to the equation MX₂(s) ⇌ M²⁺(aq) + 2 X⁻(aq), with K_sp = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ at 25°C. What is the molar solubility of MX₂ at 25°C in a 0.020 M solution of NaX, a soluble salt?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the solubility is the same in any solution picks this, the solubility in pure water from 4s³ = K_sp. The X⁻ already present raises the ion product, so much less MX₂ dissolves: s = K_sp/(0.020)² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ M.
A student who divides K_sp by [X⁻] without squaring it picks this: 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹/0.020 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ M. In K_sp = [M²⁺][X⁻]² the X⁻ term is squared, so s = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹/(0.020)² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ M.

A student who doubles the X⁻ from NaX because of the coefficient 2 in the MX₂ equation picks this: 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹/(0.040)² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ M. NaX gives one X⁻ per formula unit, so [X⁻] = 0.020 M and s = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ M.
NaX supplies [X⁻] = 0.020 M, far more than the 2s from MX₂, so K_sp = s(0.020)². Then s = (3.2 × 10⁻¹¹)/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ M, much less than the 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M solubility in pure water.
questions.explain: NaX supplies [X⁻] = 0.020 M, far more than the 2s from MX₂, so K_sp = s(0.020)². Then s = (3.2 × 10⁻¹¹)/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ M, much less than the 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M solubility in pure water.
questions.working: [X⁻] = 0.020 + 2s ≈ 0.020 M (NaX gives one X⁻ per formula unit). K_sp = [M²⁺][X⁻]² = s(0.020)² = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹, so s = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹/4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ M. 2s = 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ M ≪ 0.020 M, so the approximation holds (the exact cubic gives the same two-figure value).

questions.q: A student measures the molar solubility of four sparingly soluble salts, W, X, Y and Z, in solutions buffered at different pH values at 25°C. The graph summarizes the student's results. Based on the results, which salt is most likely a metal hydroxide such as Mg(OH)₂?
options: Salt W
Salt X
Salt Y
Salt Z
optionWhy: A student who thinks adding acid shifts a dissolution equilibrium toward the solid picks the line that rises with pH. H₃O⁺ removes OH⁻, a product of the dissolution, so a hydroxide is more soluble at low pH, not less.

Lowering the pH removes OH⁻ and raises the solubility of such a hydroxide, and raising the pH adds OH⁻, a common ion that lowers it. Only a line that falls steadily across the whole pH range, in basic as well as acidic solutions, shows this behavior.

A student who thinks pH affects a hydroxide's solubility only in acidic solution picks the line that is level above pH 7. Above pH 7 the added OH⁻ is a common ion, so a hydroxide's solubility keeps falling as the pH rises.
A student who thinks a constant K_sp means a constant solubility picks the level line. K_sp is fixed at 25°C, but H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ change [OH⁻], so a hydroxide's solubility changes with pH.
questions.explain: Lowering the pH removes OH⁻ and raises the solubility of such a hydroxide, and raising the pH adds OH⁻, a common ion that lowers it. Only a line that falls steadily across the whole pH range, in basic as well as acidic solutions, shows this behavior.
questions.working: No calculation. For a hydroxide such as Mg(OH)₂, M(OH)₂(s) ⇌ M²⁺ + 2OH⁻, H₃O⁺ removes OH⁻ at low pH (more dissolves), and added OH⁻ at high pH is a common ion (less dissolves), so the solubility falls steadily as the pH rises across the whole range. The salt whose line falls steadily from pH 0 to 14 fits.

figure.alt: Line graph. Vertical axis: Molar solubility (log scale), with no numbers. Horizontal axis: pH, with ticks at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14. Four lines, one for each salt, are labeled W, X, Y and Z at their right ends and drawn in different line styles. The line labeled W is straight, rising steadily from pH 0 to 14. The line labeled X is straight, falling steadily from pH 0 to 14. The line labeled Y is high at low pH, falls until about pH 7, then is horizontal to pH 14. The line labeled Z is horizontal at every pH.
